summary: Defines a method of computing a hash over a COSE Key. It states which fields of the key structure are included, how to build a canonical form of them, and how to hash the result, producing a thumbprint that can identify the key.

plainLanguage.summary: This makes a short fingerprint for a cryptographic key, the way a fingerprint is much smaller than a person but still points to them.

questions: how to compute a cose key thumbprint
what is a cose key thumbprint
what is the ckt confirmation method
subtitle: A fingerprint for a COSE key: hash only the required fields, in a fixed encoding, to get a stable name for the key.

tldr.problem: Applications need a short, stable way to name or select a COSE Key, but the same key can be written with different optional attributes, which would change any hash of the whole structure.
tldr.mechanism: Build a COSE_Key with only the required parameters for its key type, apply the deterministic CBOR encoding of RFC 8949, and hash the bytes (SHA-256 MUST be supported).
tldr.outcome: The thumbprint can serve as a key ID, as the proof-of-possession key reference in a CWT through the new "ckt" confirmation member, or inside a urn:ietf:params:oauth:ckt URI.

today: RFC 9679 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2024. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Thumbprint a COSE Key
sections.content:
RFC 9679 defines a method for applying a cryptographic hash function to a COSE Key structure, producing a hash value called a thumbprint. It says which fields of the key go into the hash, how to build a canonical form of those fields, and how to hash the resulting bytes.

The RFC names two main uses. One is a naming scheme for identifying or selecting the key, for example by using the thumbprint as a kid (key ID). The other is key derivation functions that mix the thumbprints of the endpoints' public keys with other application context to derive a symmetric key.

The document also adds a new CBOR Web Token (CWT) confirmation method to the IANA "CWT Confirmation Methods" registry created by RFC 8747.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine every key needs a short name tag. This document says how to make a name tag that always comes out the same for the same key, so people can find the right key quickly.

sections.title: Computing the Thumbprint
sections.content:
A thumbprint MUST be computed in three steps:

  1. Construct a COSE_Key structure (see Section 7 of RFC 9052) containing only the required parameters for the key, as listed in Section 4 of the RFC.
  2. Apply the deterministic encoding from Section 4.2.1 of RFC 8949 to that structure.
  3. Hash the resulting bytes with a cryptographic hash function H. SHA-256 is given as an example.

Implementations MUST support SHA-256 and MAY support other hash algorithms.

When several parties need to reproduce and compare a thumbprint, they must all know and use the same hash function. If only the key producer cares, for example when it uses the thumbprint as a kid, the consumer can treat the value as an opaque identifier used only for key selection.
sections.plainLanguage: First, pick out only the important parts of the key. Then write them down in one exact way, and finally squash them into a short code. Anyone who follows the same steps gets the same code.

sections.title: Required Parameters per Key Type
sections.content:
Only the required parameters of a key are used. The kty element (label 1) MUST be present for every key type, using the integer value from the IANA "COSE Key Types" registry, never a text string.

The RFC lists the required parameters for common key types. For Octet Key Pair keys such as X25519, they are kty (1), crv (-1) and x (-2). For EC2 keys such as NIST P-256 they add y (-3). RSA public keys use n (-1) and e (-2), symmetric keys use k (-1), and HSS-LMS keys use pub (-1).

For EC2 keys, implementations MUST use the uncompressed point representation, so the y-coordinate is a byte string. A compressed point MUST first be converted to the uncompressed form before the thumbprint is calculated. For other key types defined later, their defining specifications say which parameters are required.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of key has a short list of must-have parts, like a recipe with only the main ingredients. Only those go into the fingerprint.

sections.title: Design Choices and Related Thumbprints
sections.content:
Optional COSE Key parameters are left out on purpose, so that their presence or absence does not change the result. Different applications may attach different optional attributes to the same key. If those counted, one key could have many thumbprints. Leaving them out means the thumbprint refers to the key itself.

The RFC compares the result to digests of X.509 Subject Public Key Info values (Section 4.1.2.7 of RFC 5280). A COSE Key Thumbprint is logically equivalent to such a digest, except that it is computed over the CBOR representation rather than an ASN.1 one. It is less like the x5t thumbprint of a whole certificate.

The ckt of a COSE Key and the jkt of a JSON Web Key (RFC 7517) are different even for the same key material. The document does not register ckt as a JWT confirmation method or jkt as a CWT one. Keys in other formats can be thumbprinted once their COSE_Key representation is defined. Other specifications may define different thumbprints that include extra parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Leaving out the extras is like recognizing a friend by their face, not by whether they are wearing a hat today. The same friend always gets the same name tag.

sections.title: The ckt Confirmation Method and Thumbprint URIs
sections.content:
A CWT can carry a proof-of-possession key reference using the cnf claim from RFC 8747. This RFC adds a ckt member to cnf (key 5), which holds the thumbprint as a binary string. Only the thumbprint is conveyed, not the key, so the recipient must be able to obtain the identified COSE Key by using the thumbprint.

The RFC also defines URIs for thumbprints, modelled on JWK Thumbprint URIs in RFC 9278. The prefix is urn:ietf:params:oauth:ckt, followed by a colon, a hash algorithm identifier and a colon, then the thumbprint. The identifier MUST come from the "Hash Name String" column of the IANA "Named Information Hash Algorithm Registry"; a URI with an unknown identifier is not valid and applications MUST detect and handle this error. The thumbprint is base64url encoded without padding.

The text notes that "oauth" appears in the namespace only to align with JWK Thumbprint URIs; the URIs are not limited to OAuth.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of mailing the whole key, you mail just its name tag, and the receiver looks up the real key. The name tag can also be written like a web-style address so it fits in places that want one.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example starts with an EC2 P-256 key (kty 2, crv 1) that also carries a kid (label 2). The kid is not a required parameter, so it is dropped. Only kty, crv, x and y remain, in that order, and are encoded in CBOR.

Hashing with SHA-256 gives the thumbprint 496bd8afadf307e5b08c64b0421bf9dc01528a344a43bda88fadd1669da253ec. In URI form, with base64url encoding, it becomes urn:ietf:params:oauth:ckt:sha-256:SWvYr63zB-WwjGSwQhv53AFSijRKQ72oj63RZp2iU-w.
sections.plainLanguage: The example takes a key with a sticky note on it, peels the note off, and shows that the fingerprint comes only from the key parts that matter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A thumbprint identifies a key uniquely only if a single unambiguous COSE Key representation is defined and used for the computation. Key identifiers are not part of the calculation. If a particular application needs certain optional parameters to be covered, this specification would not be suitable.

Comparing thumbprints is not a reliable way to exclude particular keys, because an attacker can supply a transformation of a key that looks different. The RFC's example is an RSA key with modulus N and a modified key with modulus 3*N, which would still work about 1/3 of the time.

Thumbprints of symmetric keys need care. Developers MUST ensure sufficient entropy so attackers cannot precompute tables of keys and hashes; a randomly selected key of at least 128 bits is given as safe. Thumbprints MUST NOT be used with passwords or other low-entropy secrets, and if sufficient entropy cannot be assured, symmetric key thumbprints MUST NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: A fingerprint tells you which key it is, but a tricky person can sneak in a lookalike. And a fingerprint of a weak secret is dangerous, because someone can guess the secret and check it against the fingerprint.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA added the ckt entry to the "CWT Confirmation Methods" registry: description "COSE Key SHA-256 Thumbprint", confirmation key 5, value type binary string, with no JWT confirmation method name.

IANA also added urn:ietf:params:oauth:ckt, with common name "COSE Key Thumbprint URI", to the "OAuth URI" registry created by RFC 6755. The change controller for both is the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of names got two new entries, one for the name tag in tokens and one for the address style, so nobody else reuses them.
